pages.description: AI automation without the surprises. Describe a recurring job in plain words, and get a workflow you can read, that runs the same way every time and checks with you before anything goes out.

sections.excerpt: BookOpen, Bot, CalendarClock, Cloud, Code, FileText, Inbox, MessageSquare, Rocket, Server, WandSparkles, Workflow, } from 'lucide-react'; SynapseOrch turns the jobs your team repeats every week into workflows that run themselves — the report, the triage, the brief, the review. You describe the job in plain words, it builds the workflow, and a person signs off wherever the output leaves the…
Tell Synapse AI the job in plain words, or start from a template. It draws the workflow: the steps, the model for each, and where a person signs off.
sections.heading: Describe it

sections.excerpt: Read the workflow on the canvas before it runs. Change any prompt, tool or model, and put a human step wherever the output leaves the building. Tool policy decides which tool calls need a yes first.
sections.heading: Approve it

sections.excerpt: Run it on a schedule, from a chat message or through the API. Every run takes the same path, and the logs show what each step did and what it cost.
sections.heading: Rely on it

sections.excerpt: A workflow is a fixed path of steps, and execution follows it — no detours the model invents on the way. Where the next action is already known, Tool and LLM steps skip the agent loop entirely: no reasoning overhead, the same shape of output every time, and far cheaper. When a step fails, the run says so instead of carrying on as if it worked.
sections.heading: Same path, every run [#workflows-that-do-exactly-what-you-designed]

sections.excerpt: Human steps pause a run and wait — for minutes or for days — then resume exactly where they stopped when someone answers, in the app or from a chat app. Runs survive restarts, and on Cloud, time spent waiting for a person never costs a credit.
sections.heading: Nothing goes out without a yes [#never-blocked-on-a-human-decision]

sections.excerpt: Every step names its model. A small, fast one routes and classifies; a strong one handles only the steps that need judgement; and some steps need no model at all. On Cloud, a plan stops at its allowance, and nothing is billed past it; managed models draw from a prepaid wallet.
sections.heading: The bill stops where you set it [#cut-costs-without-cutting-quality]

sections.excerpt: The engine is open source under AGPL-3.0, and Cloud runs the same one. Your workflows can always move to your own servers, with no licence check and nothing sent to us — nobody can switch them off. OpenTelemetry export to your own collector is there if you want it, and off by default.
sections.heading: Yours to keep

sections.excerpt: Fourteen-plus hosted providers, local models through Ollama, and CLI mode for Claude, Gemini and Codex with no API key at all. Switch an agent's model in the middle of a conversation and it keeps its prompt, memory, tools and plan. On Cloud, managed models need no key.
sections.heading: Any model, switch any time [#no-lock-in-on-models]

sections.excerpt: - Python → dropped in, it runs sandboxed - Any REST API → describe the schema, or import an OpenAPI spec - Any MCP server → local subprocess or remote HTTP - Any workflow → promote it to an agent and nest it inside another

pages.title: Introduction

pages.description: Four kinds of agent — conversational, code, orchestrator and Team — and which one a given job actually wants.

sections.excerpt: Every agent has a type, chosen when you create it. The type decides what the agent does with a message. | Type | What it does | |---|---| | Conversational | A general-purpose assistant with configurable tools | | Code | A conversational agent that also searches indexed repositories | | Orchestrator | Runs a linked workflow instead of conversing | | Team | A lead that sends work to its members…
The default, and the right answer for most work — research, writing, analysis, support. It keeps full multi-turn history and runs the ReAct loop against whatever tools you gave it.
sections.heading: Conversational

sections.excerpt: A conversational agent with repositories and database connections attached. It can search code semantically before reading or editing, which is what makes it useful on a codebase too large to put in a prompt. Assign its repos and DB configs in the agent editor; configure them under Settings → Repos and Settings → DB configs. See Code repositories.
sections.heading: Code

sections.excerpt: Wraps a workflow. Sending it a message triggers that workflow rather than starting a conversation, which lets you expose a multi-step pipeline as something that looks like a chat. It still keeps the conversation: the recent turns reach the workflow's model steps, and its answer is what the workflow made (the workflow's Result). An Orchestrator agent is made with Deploy as Agent on the workflow…

sections.excerpt: A lead with members: other agents of yours, each with its own tools and approvals. The lead answers small questions itself and hands bigger or parallel work to its members, one at a time (it waits for each) or as a team (they work in parallel and share a task list), then answers with what they found. The API and exported files store this type as delegate. Use a Team agent when you want one entry…

A helper runs with a subset of the agent's tools and returns; several can work at once from one response, and in the app's chat one can work in the background. See Helpers. | | Use when | |---|---| | Team agent | The specialists are durable, configured agents the lead routes…

It reports "cancelling", never "cancelled", and the distinction is honest rather than pedantic: a turn sitting inside a long provider call stops when that call returns, not the instant you click. A bash command already running is not stopped either; it runs to its own timeout. If nothing was running — the turn had already finished — that is reported as such…

sections.excerpt: A helper is a short-lived agent that one of your agents makes for a single task: look these three suppliers up, summarise this document, check that order. It works with some of the agent's own tools, answers, and is gone. It is the quick way to split work in parallel without setting up a Team agent.

In the agent's setup, under Limits, turn on Can send helpers. The agent can then hand a focused task to a helper with the spawnsubtask tool. (A workflow agent runs its workflow, so it has no such switch.) Helper model says what its helpers run on: - Same as this agent, the default; - Quick-step model, the workspace's Model for quick steps from Settings › Models, for cheap small work; - or any…

It never gets a tool the agent's tool policy blocks or would ask about, and the agent is told which it held back and why: Not given to the sub-agent: runbash (it needs a person's approval — call it yourself and they will be asked). In the app's chat, an agent can also send a helper to work in the background: the agent's turn ends and the conversation is free, the helper's line stays in the chat with Stop, and when the helper finishes its result comes back to the agent once, marked as From your helper…

sections.excerpt: Long conversations eventually exceed the context window. Auto context compaction is on by default and fires at autocompactthreshold (80,000 characters), first by trimming the oldest tool outputs and then, if that is not enough, by summarising. The pre-compaction history is archived to the vault, so nothing is lost. ---

The user message is combined with the system prompt, the tool list, and conversation history, then sent to the LLM. 2. The LLM produces a response that may include one or more tool calls. 3. If there are tool calls, SynapseOrch executes them and feeds the results back to the LLM. 4. This repeats until…

pages.description: Reusable instruction packages an agent loads on demand — nearly free until the moment it actually uses one.

sections.excerpt: A skill is a package of instructions an agent can load when it needs it: a house style, a review checklist, the steps for a deploy, the shape of your API. Instead of stuffing all of that into a system prompt that is paid for on every turn, an agent carries only the names of its skills and pulls a body in when the work calls for it. Skills live under Build → Agents → Skills, and you assign them…

SynapseOrch uses Claude Code's skill format, deliberately — YAML frontmatter carrying name and description, then a markdown body: That shape is already on disk in thousands of repositories, so a skill written for one product works in the other and nobody has to maintain a converter. Unknown frontmatter keys are kept but ignored, for the same reason. | Limit | Value | |---|---| | Name | 64…
sections.heading: The format

sections.excerpt: Progressive disclosure is the whole design: - Every turn an agent pays only for its skills' names and one-line descriptions — the roster. - The body enters the context once, through the native loadskill tool, and only when the agent decides it needs it. So giving an agent twenty skills costs twenty lines of prompt, not twenty documents. Write descriptions that make the choice obvious — the…

The disk is .agents/skills/ scanned at the install root, plus whatever SYNAPSESKILLSDIR points at. It is read-only, so skills already sitting on the machine are offered without an import step. pages.description: Connect Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs and Sheets in one click — no OAuth client to register.

sections.excerpt: On SynapseOrch Cloud, Google Workspace is a platform connection: open Apps, click Connect Google on the Google Workspace card, approve the scopes Google shows you, and your agents can use Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs and Sheets. There is no Google Cloud project to create and no OAuth client to register. That is the main practical difference from self-hosting, where the credential belongs to…

Google shows you the scopes at consent time, and they are the ones the tools actually need — SynapseOrch does not ask for broader access than the tools it exposes. The connection belongs to the person who authorised it. What agents can then do is bounded by that person's own Google permissions: connecting does not grant an agent access to anything you could not open yourself.
sections.heading: What you are approving

sections.excerpt: Delete the Google Workspace server under Apps (Connected on its card opens it), or revoke SynapseOrch from your Google account permissions. Either takes effect immediately; agents that were using those tools start failing that step rather than falling back to anything.
sections.heading: Revoking

sections.excerpt: Once connected, the Google tools appear like any other tool — tick them on an agent, or call them from a Tool step. Because these tools reach a system outside the workspace and can modify real data — sending mail, editing documents — they are a good first candidate for tool policy. Setting destructive to confirm puts you in the loop before an agent sends anything.
sections.heading: Using it

sections.excerpt: A connection is currently shared at the organisation level rather than being per-member: agents act as the account that authorised it, not as whoever triggered the run. If you need an agent to act as each individual user, that is not available yet — connect a dedicated account rather than a personal one.

Owners and admins decide which roles hear about each event, in the app and by email, and each person can turn off what reaches them. Both live under Settings → Notifications. What the bell is and how a run raises a notification are on Notifications. This page covers what Cloud adds: roles, email, and approvals from scheduled agents.

Content you put into SynapseOrch Cloud — prompts, documents, run inputs and outputs — is not used to train models, ours or anyone else's. Platform models run against providers under terms that exclude training on customer data.

sections.excerpt: Each organisation's data is scoped to that organisation throughout — storage, runs and model calls. Provider keys are read for each run and never written into the process environment, so they are not inherited by the subprocesses the engine spawns, including MCP servers and the code sandbox. That is the same boundary as self-hosting.

pages.description: SynapseOrch has two independent caches that together cut LLM cost without changing what your agents do. Most of it runs automatically — you only need to know where to look in the UI to see savings, and which knob to flip when you want stronger caching on a specific orchestration step.

The prompt cache piggybacks on each LLM provider's native caching mechanism. SynapseOrch injects cachecontrol markers (Anthropic, Bedrock) or relies on automatic prefix caching (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Gemini) so that the long, stable parts of your system prompt — agent instructions, tool definitions, RAG context — are reused across turns instead of being re-tokenised every call. pages.description: Name a set of related tools so forty imported endpoints behave like one thing you can reason about.

sections.excerpt: A tool group is a name for a set of related tools. It exists mostly because importing an OpenAPI spec can create dozens of tools at once, and a flat list of forty endpoints is not something anyone can work with. Groups are managed on the Tools screen: pick or create one in a tool's Group field, and each OpenAPI import creates its own. Each custom tool belongs to at most one.

- Assigning. Tick a group when configuring an agent instead of ticking its members one at a time. - Reading. The tools list stays navigable when one vendor's API contributes forty entries. - Auditing. "Which agents can reach the billing API" is a question about a group.
sections.heading: What groups are for

sections.excerpt: Deleting a group does not delete its tools — they stay and become ungrouped. The group is a label, not a container, and losing a label should never lose the thing it was on.
sections.heading: Deleting a group

sections.excerpt: A group is organisational. It does not restrict what its tools may do, and putting a dangerous tool in a group named "read-only" changes nothing. What an agent may actually do with the tools it holds is tool policy, which decides per call and by declared behaviour rather than by name.
sections.heading: Groups are not a permission boundary

sections.excerpt: A workflow that runs without erroring has not necessarily done its job well. Evals answer the other question: was the output any good, and is it getting worse? You write a rubric, bind it to a workflow, and every finished run is scored. Two rules decide whether a score is worth interrupting you about. To measure how well a knowledge base finds its answers, see Evaluate a knowledge base — a…

Defaults to 0–10 | | Floor | An absolute line — below this is a regression | | Drop | A fall this far below the recent mean is a regression | | Baseline runs | How many recent runs the mean is taken over. Defaults to 10 | | Judge model |…
sections.heading: The rubric

sections.excerpt: One model call scores one finished run against one rubric — deliberately one call, not one per criterion and not one per step. The model returns an overall score, a score per criterion and a score per step in a single structured answer. That choice is about three things, in the order they mattered: cost is the whole argument for this product over an autonomous framework, and N calls per run is…

sections.excerpt: Two rules, because they catch different failures: - Floor — an absolute line. Answers is this good enough, and is the only rule that works on a brand-new workflow with no history. - Drop — a fall below the mean of recent runs. Answers did this get worse, and catches the slow slide from 9.0 to 7.5 that never crosses any absolute line and is what you actually meet in practice. The floor is checked…

Harbor & Pine's operations team reads a supplier review every Monday. Nobody writes it: Monday supplier review runs the Weekly supplier review workflow at 07:00 UTC each Monday, and the review is waiting when the team arrives.

pages.description: Make an agent: its model, its instructions and the tools it may use. Then give it a skill, a set of instructions it loads only when a task needs them.

sections.excerpt: An agent is a model with a system prompt and a set of tools. Given a task, it decides its own next step — search, call a tool, read the result, try again — until it has an answer or reaches its turn limit. You talk to an agent in Chat, and a workflow's Agent step hands it one part of a job. This guide makes the kind of agent Harbor & Pine's Order desk is: one that answers stockists' questions…

Open Agents and press New agent. Fill in its Name and a one-line Description. The description is shown in the list and when a workflow's Agent step picks an agent, so write it for the person choosing an agent: Answers stockists' questions about orders, shipping rules and payment terms, with citations.
sections.heading: Name it and say what it does

sections.excerpt: Keep Type on Conversational, the everyday agent with its own tools; Agent Types covers the others. Under Model, leave the workspace default or choose one for this agent. A cheap model is right for routing and short answers; give a stronger one to an agent whose answers people rely on. The Order desk runs on Nova Lite.

sections.excerpt: Every tool gives it everything the workspace has except the SQL tools; Choose specific tools lets you tick exactly what it may call. Narrow is better: an agent offered fewer tools picks the right one more often, and cannot call what it was never given. The Order desk needs only getdatetime and its knowledge bases. Leave Planning on for agents that take several steps: the agent keeps a task list…

sections.excerpt: Under Tool policy, the agent follows the workspace's tool policy unless you choose otherwise here: Allow, Ask first or Block for each kind of tool — tools that change data permanently, tools that reach outside this workspace, and tools that don't say what they do, which is most of them.

The Order desk answers from Compliance guides and Suppliers & invoices. - Skills — instructions it loads when a task calls for them (below). - Channels — the Telegram bots it answers on (and Slack or Discord, self-hosted), once you connect one. - Memory — off…

Check it under Preview. Type @ to put a Vault file in the prompt as @[path], read fresh each time the agent runs, and {{ for a variable. The Order desk's: Say what it should do when it does not know. An agent carries every skill's one-line description in its prompt, and reads a skill's full instructions only when a task calls for it, so ten skills cost ten lines until one is needed. Use a skill for instructions several agents share, or ones too long to carry on every turn.

sections.excerpt: Chat is the quickest way to try an agent: ask what its users will ask, and watch what it does. It is also how people use an agent day to day, and the same agent answers the same way on your website widget and in Slack or Telegram.
Open Chat. Choose who to talk to with the agent's name at the foot of the message box. The agent is fixed for the conversation once it starts; press New Conversation to talk to another.

sections.excerpt: If the tool policy says Ask first for a call the agent wants to make, the turn stops and asks: Permission needed, with Allow once and Refuse, and a box for why. Allowing runs that one call, with those arguments, and the turn carries on. Refusing tells the agent, which works around it. Sending a new message instead of answering refuses the call: the card reads You moved on — this was not run.

pages.description: Write a rubric, have a judge model score every run against it, hear when a score falls, and re-run a fixed set of questions after every change.

sections.excerpt: A run that finished without an error has not necessarily done its job well. Evals answer the other question: was the answer any good, and is it getting worse? You describe what good looks like in a rubric, a judge model scores every finished run against it, and a run that scores badly is flagged. Harbor & Pine scores every run of Answer a customer question, because those answers go to stockists.

Open Runs › Evals and press New rubric. Give it a Name — Customer answer quality — and under What the judge should keep in mind, the context that applies to every criterion: How well an answer to a stockist's question serves them.
sections.heading: Name it and set the scene

sections.excerpt: Press Add criterion for each thing to judge, with guidance the judge can check. Accurate judges nothing; every claim comes from the cited passages judges something. Harbor & Pine's four: | Criterion | Guidance | |---|---| | Grounded | Every claim comes from the cited passages. | | Answers the question | Says what the stockist should expect or do. | | Tone | Plain, courteous, no jargon. | |…
sections.heading: Add criteria

sections.excerpt: - Scale max — the top of the scale; 10 by default. - Floor — a score below this is flagged, however the run did before. It is the rule that guards a new workflow with no history. Harbor & Pine's is 6. - Drop — a fall this far below the mean of recent runs is flagged: the slow slide from 9 to 7.5 that never crosses the floor. It waits for three scores before it says anything. Leave either empty to…
sections.heading: Say what counts as a bad score

sections.excerpt: Open the workflow in the editor, open Workflow settings, and under Guardrails choose the rubric in Score runs against. Save. From now on each run is judged when it finishes: one model call per run, which can never fail the run it scores. If the workflow has runs from before, open the rubric, pick the workflow and press Score earlier runs, so the floor and the trend have something to work with…
sections.heading: Bind it to the workflow

sections.excerpt: Open the rubric and choose the workflow in Scores for: its latest score, its average, the trend, and the recent runs with each one's score, the ones that broke the floor or the drop flagged. Rate a scored run with the thumbs to say whether you agree with the judge. A rubric that people keep disagreeing with needs better guidance.

sections.excerpt: Every time a workflow runs, SynapseOrch keeps the run: each step's output, the shared state it left, the exact prompts the models were sent, and what it cost. This guide reads Harbor & Pine's runs — one that finished, one waiting for a person, and one that failed — and then where the money went.

Runs lists every workflow run, newest first and grouped by day, including the ones a schedule or the API started. Pick Needs you, Running, Queued, Failed, Completed or Cancelled at the top to show only those runs, and Search runs… to find one by its workflow's name or its run ID. A row's menu stops a run, replays a failed one, or copies its ID. Click a run to open it. Home puts the ones that need…
sections.heading: Find a run

sections.excerpt: A run's page shows how long it took, its tokens and its model cost across the top. Below them: - The path — one row per step, with its type, status, cost and time, and what started the run. Open a step for what it wrote, the models it called and the tools it used. - What it produced — the run's result. - Activity — the run's events as they happen; it streams while the run works. - Shared state —…
sections.heading: Read a run

sections.excerpt: A Human step pauses the run and asks. The run reads Needs input, and the question is on its page, on Home, under Waiting on you in the menu and in notifications. Answer it where you see it: here, write a Note for the ledger if you like and press Approve payment or Decline. A question with fields of its own takes them and Send answer. The answer is written to state and the run carries on from the…
sections.heading: Answer a run waiting for a person

sections.excerpt: A run that did not complete says why at the top — Why it stopped: … — and the step that failed is marked on the path with its error. Here, the invoice was sent with its lines under items, and Check totals reads lines: the input was wrong, not the workflow. Replay resumes a failed run from the step that failed, keeping what the steps before it did. Use it when the failure was passing — a provider…
sections.heading: Find out why a run failed

sections.excerpt: Each plan runs a set number of runs at once. A run started while they are all busy waits its turn: it reads Queued, 2nd in line, moves up on its own, and starts as soon as a slot frees. Time in line is not charged, and Cancel works while it waits. See Capacity.
sections.heading: Queued runs

sections.excerpt: On SynapseOrch Cloud a run draws on two separate balances: - Execution credits, from your plan, pay for the steps. A step is priced by its type: an Agent, LLM or Tool step is 1 credit; a Retrieve, Transform, If / Else or other logic step 0.1; a Human step nothing. Answer a customer question — one Retrieve and one LLM step — costs 1.1 credits. A run that works for minutes is charged at least one…

sections.excerpt: - Runs › Logs holds the full transcript of each run and each agent call: the system prompt, the context at every turn, each tool call with its result. Search by name, run ID or input. See Full Execution Logs. - The bell lists runs that finished, failed or stopped to ask a question. Settings → Notifications chooses what reaches each role, in the app and by email. See Notifications and Email. Runs…

pages.description: Choose the models your agents use, set the values tools and prompts share, and decide which tool calls need a yes first.

sections.excerpt: Three settings shape everything you build afterwards: which model an agent uses when it names none, the shared values your tools and prompts read, and which tool calls run without asking. Each takes a minute. Settings is at the foot of the menu. A new workspace's Home opens on Getting started, the path to a first workflow: connect a model, build a workflow from a template or with Synapse AI, run…

Open Settings → Models. Under Defaults, choose the Default model: every agent and step that names no model of its own uses it. Harbor & Pine uses Nova Micro, a cheap SynapseOrch model, and gives the two agents that answer people Nova Lite.
sections.heading: Pick a default model

sections.excerpt: - Builder model — what Synapse AI runs on. A build is a long multi-step run, so a stronger model can pay for itself here even when your agents run on a cheap one. Unset, it follows the default. - Reasoning — how hard a model thinks when an agent does not say. Thinking is billed as output. - Embedding model — what turns text into vectors, for searching by meaning: code search and each workflow…
sections.heading: Decide on the rest, or leave them

sections.excerpt: SynapseOrch models need no key: they are paid per token from the model wallet. To use your own account with a provider instead, open it under Providers, paste the key into API key and press Save. Its models then appear in every model picker, billed by the provider, not the wallet. You can mix both: one agent on a SynapseOrch model, another on your key. There are no SynapseOrch models: every model…
sections.heading: Bring your own keys, if you want to

sections.excerpt: A variable is a value you set once and use everywhere as { }: in a tool's URL, headers or body, an agent's system prompt, or a step's prompt. Change it here and everything that reads it follows.
sections.heading: Set values tools and prompts share

sections.excerpt: Open Settings → Variables and press Add variable. Give it a name of letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores, not starting with a digit, and a value. Harbor & Pine keeps its approval limit, APAPPROVALLIMIT = 5000, and the address stockists write to, SUPPORTEMAIL.
sections.heading: Add the variable

sections.excerpt: For an API token or a password, tick the box beside the value. A secret is stored encrypted and never shown again: once saved it reads Secret set, and Replace gives it a new value.
sections.heading: Mark credentials secret

sections.excerpt: Press Save variables. In a prompt, { } becomes orders@harborpine.example when the agent or step runs. Variables come back as plain text on a self-hosted install: keep secrets in a provider's key field or a tool's own settings, not here. See Variables.
sections.heading: Save, then use it

sections.excerpt: Some tools act on the world: they send an email, write a file, call an outside API. Under Settings → General → Tool policy, choose for each kind of tool whether a call runs (Allow), waits for a person to approve it (Ask first) or never runs (Block). An agent can set its own policy in its editor, which overrides the workspace's for that agent. A call waiting for a yes appears in chat, on the run's…

pages.description: What an agent can reach — built-in tools, your own HTTP and Python tools, apps you connect over MCP, files in the Vault — and how to add each.

sections.excerpt: An agent can only do what its tools let it. A tool is a function the model may call, with a name, a description it reads to decide when to call it, and a schema for its arguments. There are four kinds: | Kind | What it is | Where | |---|---|---| | Built-in | Read and write Vault files, run Python, scrape or drive a web page, read a PDF or a spreadsheet, query a database, tell the time | Every…
Harbor & Pine's nettermsduedate works out when an invoice falls due. A model is unreliable at date arithmetic; three lines of Python are not.
sections.heading: Write a tool of your own

sections.excerpt: Open Apps › Tools, press New tool and choose Python code (or HTTP request, below). The Name is what the model calls, so keep it a plain identifier: nettermsduedate. The Description is how the model decides when to call it; say what it does and what it needs: > Works out when an invoice is due from its date and payment terms (net-15, net-30 or net-45).
sections.heading: Name it and describe it

sections.excerpt: Under Input schema, list what the model must pass, as JSON Schema. The descriptions matter: they are all the model knows about each argument.
sections.heading: Describe its arguments

sections.excerpt: The arguments arrive as args, and whatever the code prints is the tool's answer: The code runs in a sandbox, with the common data packages installed. On SynapseOrch Cloud, Python tools run on the Team and Business plans.
sections.heading: Write the code

sections.excerpt: Press Create. Then open the agent that should use it — the Invoice clerk — and tick it under Choose specific tools. An HTTP tool is the same with a method and URL in place of code: the model's arguments fill the URL and body, and Add header carries credentials, stored encrypted. Put a value that several tools share in a variable and write { } where it goes. If the API has an OpenAPI document…
sections.heading: Create it and give it to an agent

sections.excerpt: An app brings all its tools at once, from its MCP server. Once its tools are found, every agent in the workspace can be given them.
sections.heading: Connect an app over MCP

sections.excerpt: Open Apps and press Add server to browse the directory, or search it. Each app says what connecting needs: Sign in on the app's own page, or No account needed.
sections.heading: Pick the app

sections.excerpt: Press Connect and finish what the app asks: approve it on its sign-in screen, or paste an access token and press Connect. For a server that is not listed, choose Add another server and enter its name and HTTPS URL.
sections.heading: Connect it

sections.excerpt: Select the server to see its status and the tools it offers; Discover tools reads them again after the app changes. Then give the tools to the agents that need them. Google Workspace has its own button, Connect Google: Gmail, Calendar, Sheets and Docs for every agent, as one Google account an admin connects. See Connecting Google Workspace. A self-hosted install connects apps' MCP servers on Apps…
sections.heading: Check its tools

sections.excerpt: The Vault holds files your agents read: notes, data, documents. Upload files or press New file for Markdown, plain text, JSON or CSV, in folders. Then: - Put a file in a prompt. Type @ in an agent's system prompt or a step's prompt and pick the file; it goes in as @[path], and its contents are read fresh each time the agent runs. Right for a short file needed on every turn: a price list, a style…

pages.description: How a workflow is built: steps in an order you choose, shared state that carries each step's result to the next, routes, people and guardrails.

sections.excerpt: A workflow has a fixed path. Each step does one thing, reads what it needs from the run's shared state, and writes its result back for the steps after it. The path is yours, so every run of a workflow goes the same way: you can read what each step did, and its cost hardly varies from run to run. Harbor & Pine has four. This guide reads one of them, Invoice triage, step by step; the next builds…

Invoice triage checks a supplier's invoice, asks accounts payable to approve anything over $5,000 or from a supplier not yet approved, then drafts the note for the ledger: 1. Check totals, a Transform step, runs a few lines of Python over state.invoice, which the run was started with (the API passes it as initialstate): adds up the lines, compares the total with the limit and the supplier with…

The run strip at the bottom left follows each step as it lights up, and its Run Log opens what…

See Templates and Setup. - Synapse AI — in the menu on every page, or Build with AI on the Workflows page. Describe the job, and it draws the workflow for you to read and change before it runs. pages.description: Bring your team into the workspace, give each person the role they need, and see who did what: roles, seats, sessions, notifications and the audit log.

sections.excerpt: Everything on SynapseOrch Cloud belongs to a workspace (an organisation): agents, workflows, runs, usage and billing. People are members of it, each with one role. Harbor & Pine has three — Riley, the owner, Sam, who builds the workflows, and Priya, who reads the results — and an invitation out to Jordan.

Roles are ordered: each can do everything the one before it can. | Role | Can | Harbor & Pine | |---|---|---| | Viewer | Read everything — workflows, runs, results — and change nothing. Cannot start a run, chat, or answer a run or an approval | Priya, in operations, reads the Monday review | | Approver | Everything a viewer can, plus answer a run waiting for a person and a tool call waiting for…
sections.heading: Choose each person's role

sections.excerpt: Open Settings → Members. Under Invite someone, enter their Email address, pick a Role and press Send invite. Only admins and owners can invite, and only an owner can invite an owner.
sections.heading: Send the invitation

sections.excerpt: The invitation is listed under Pending invitations, with whether the email was delivered and when it expires. Resend it, or revoke it; an invitation expires after seven days, and resending it sends a fresh link with seven more. Someone with a SynapseOrch account joins straight away when they accept; someone new makes an account first.
sections.heading: Follow it

sections.excerpt: Change a member's role in their row, or remove them; removing someone ends their access at once. Making someone a viewer frees their builder's place immediately. At the plan's limit. Each plan allows a number of people who can build, counting pending invitations as builder, admin or owner that have not expired. Members says where you stand: 3 of 100 people who can build, counting invitations…
sections.heading: Change roles as people's work changes

sections.excerpt: Settings → Notifications sets, for the whole workspace, which roles hear about each event — a run that failed, a run waiting for an answer, a payment problem — in the app and by email. An admin or owner changes it. Under For you, each person turns off anything they would rather not get. See Notifications and Email.
sections.heading: Decide who hears about what

sections.excerpt: - Sessions. Settings → Sessions lists the devices you are signed in on: when each began, when it was last used, its IP address and device. If you see one you do not recognise, press Sign out everywhere; it ends every session, this one included. - The audit log. On the Business plan, owners and admins download the workspace's audit records — every invitation, role change, setting, key and run…
sections.heading: Keep the workspace safe

sections.excerpt: A person can belong to several workspaces; Switch workspace, under the workspace's name at the top of the menu, lists them. Nothing is shared between them — separate workflows, runs and billing — so keep a separate workspace for a real boundary, such as a client's work. Next: the wallet and plans — what the workspace pays for, and how.

pages.description: SynapseOrch supports portable bundle files that contain agents, orchestrations, and MCP server configurations. Use them to share your work, back up configurations, or deploy across environments.

sections.excerpt: A bundle is a single JSON file containing: - Agent definitions (system prompts, tool lists, model overrides) - Workflow DAGs (steps, edges, guardrails) - MCP server configurations - Custom tool definitions Vault files and conversation history are not included — bundles are configuration-only. Knowledge bases are not included either. An agent's bases and a Retrieve or Ingest step's base travel by…

pages.description: Put one of your agents on your own website with a single script tag — origin-locked, rate-limited, and rendered in an iframe so nothing leaks either way.

sections.excerpt: A widget publishes one agent to one or more websites. Visitors chat with it without signing in to anything. That is the whole integration. Create the widget under Channels › Widgets, pick the agent, add the sites allowed to embed it, and copy the tag.

The loader creates an iframe and talks to it. It deliberately does not draw the chat into your page, and the reasons are worth knowing because they are what makes it safe to paste onto a customer-facing site: - Your page cannot read the conversation or the visitor's token. The iframe is a separate browsing context with no access from the host page. A widget drawn into your own DOM would hand both…
sections.heading: How it renders

sections.excerpt: The public key says which widget. The origin allow-list says whether the page asking for it may have it, and it is the only thing standing between a scraped key and your model bill. It is enforced twice, because the two points fail in opposite directions: - Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors on the embed page. The browser refuses to paint the frame, so a key pasted onto a site you did not…
sections.heading: Who is allowed to embed it

sections.excerpt: The allow-list is the front door. Limits are the floor underneath it, for what the door cannot cover: a forged Referer, a script driving a browser on a page you do allow, or simply a popular site where the traffic is legitimate and still more than you meant to pay for. | Counter | Limit | Answers | |---|---|---| | Messages per visitor IP | 20 in 5 minutes | One person hammering the widget | | New…
sections.heading: Rate limits

sections.excerpt: A closed vocabulary, not free CSS — the widget renders on somebody else's website, and every option has to keep looking right at 320px wide, in both colour schemes, next to whatever else is on the page. | Option | Values | |---|---| | Theme | auto, light, dark | | Font | system, sans, serif, rounded, mono | | Header | accent, neutral | | Launcher | bubble, logo | | Position | right, left | |…

sections.excerpt: A visitor does not get the agent's tools. Under What visitors can use, tick the tools a visitor's turn may use — nothing is ticked until you tick it, and anyone on the sites you allowed can make the agent use a ticked tool, so a read-only one reads your files and data for them. Each tool carries a badge for what it does: Changes data, Reaches outside, Reads your data, Does not say what it does.…

sections.excerpt: A visitor gets a session and a token scoped to that widget, and history within their own session. They cannot reach anything else in your workspace — the widget endpoints are a separate, narrow surface, unrelated to the API keys that drive /api/v1 and /api/v2. A visitor talking to a workflow agent sees the run's answer, never each step's output. A visitor who clicks to another page on your site…

pages.description: SynapseOrch can index code repositories and give agents the ability to search them semantically and lexically.

sections.excerpt: Agents describe what they want in plain language and receive file names, line numbers, and relevant code snippets. They can also grep, glob, and read line ranges — see Code Search for the full tool list.

1. You add a repo by its absolute path on the server. 2. SynapseOrch walks the directory tree and splits files into overlapping chunks, following each language's structure where it can. 3. Each chunk is embedded with your embedding model and stored in PostgreSQL + pgvector. 4. Agents call the code search toolkit (searchcodebase, grep, glob, …) at run time. 5. SynapseOrch returns ranked chunks for…
sections.heading: How it works

sections.excerpt: - PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension - An Embedding model selected in Settings → Models. There is no default — indexing fails with "Embedding model is not configured" until one is set. See Embedding models.
sections.heading: Prerequisites

sections.excerpt: In Settings → General, toggle Code repository indexing on. SynapseOrch inspects your machine and shows the right next step: | What SynapseOrch finds | What it shows | |---|---| | Working PostgreSQL with pgvector | Nothing more — you're done | | PostgreSQL not installed | OS-specific install instructions | | No database configured | A form for host, port, username, password, database name. Click…

Names match anywhere; paths…

sections.excerpt: Saving a repository starts indexing straight away, as long as the path exists and Code repository indexing is on — there is no separate Index button. The card shows the status: — or stopping, stopped or error. While it runs, the card counts chunks indexed so far. Stop indexing cancels it. Large repos (10k+ files) may take several minutes.

Just before the Google Workspace server starts, they are written to a temporary folder that the server reads; nothing there needs backing up. sections.excerpt: One behaviour is specific to the gateway. When it refuses a call over quota or balance — an HTTP 402 — the gateway's own sentence is passed through rather than replaced with a generic error. That is deliberate: the figures are in that sentence. "Insufficient balance: $0.12 remaining, this call needs $0.40" is actionable from a run log; "the gateway refused" is not.

pages.title: Notifications

pages.description: Every run keeps an append-only event journal, so closing the tab does not lose the stream and a crash does not lose the run.

sections.excerpt: A run emits events as it goes — steps starting, tool calls, agent output. Those events are journaled, which buys two things: you can close a tab mid-run and pick the stream back up, and a run that is interrupted resumes from where it stopped rather than from the beginning.

Every event is appended to a per-run journal as one line, each carrying a monotonic sequence id. When you reopen a run that is still going, the UI replays from the journal and then continues live — so you see what you missed rather than joining midway. The sequence id is written into the line rather than derived from its position in the file. That is what makes a crash cheap: a torn final line…
sections.heading: Reattaching to a running run

sections.excerpt: A single process reads the journal directly. Scale mode publishes the same events to a Redis stream instead, because the reader and the worker are different processes. The read endpoints serve whichever of the two exists for a run, so the behaviour you see is identical.
sections.heading: In scale mode

sections.excerpt: It lives in scratch storage and is deliberately not published to the blob store when a run closes — it is read by the live-tail endpoint while the run is in flight, and in scale mode the Redis stream already answers across processes. Writing it out afterwards would be amplification for data nothing reads. Two limits follow from that, and both matter if you are tempted to treat the journal as a…
sections.heading: What the journal is not

sections.excerpt: Because state is checkpointed rather than held in memory, a run survives things that would otherwise end it: - Human gates — a run waiting for a person survives a restart and resumes when they answer. - Tool approvals — a call held for confirmation checkpoints the same way. - Mid-step interruption — a run picks up at the step boundary it reached, not at the start.

pages.description: A human gate is an orchestration step that pauses execution and waits for a human to provide input before continuing. This enables approval workflows, data collection, review processes, and any scenario where a human decision is required mid-pipeline.

The answer is written to state 5. Execution continues from the step after the gate The paused state is checkpointed to the store, so the run survives a backend restart and resumes where it stopped. pages.description: The code search tool gives agents semantic and lexical access to indexed repositories. pages.description: The Excel parser tool reads .xlsx files and converts their contents to Markdown tables. Agents can then analyse, summarise, or extract data from spreadsheets without needing to execute code.

sections.excerpt: Downloads an Excel file from a URL and returns its sheets as Markdown tables.
sections.heading: Tool: parsexlsx [#tool-parseexcel]

sections.excerpt: | Argument | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | fileurl | string | URL of the .xlsx file (required) | Every sheet is parsed, whole; there is no sheet or row argument.
sections.heading: Arguments

sections.excerpt: For each sheet, in order: a --- Sheet: --- marker, then the sheet as a Markdown table with its column headers in the first row — or [Empty Sheet]. If the download or parsing fails, the call fails — Error parsing XLSX: … with the reason — and a Tool step that made it fails with that reason; it is never the tool's output.
sections.heading: Output

sections.excerpt: The file is fetched over HTTP from the SynapseOrch server, so it cannot be a local path or a Vault file. A host on your own network — loopback, private or link-local addresses, including where a redirect leads — is refused unless it is listed in EGRESSALLOWHOSTS. A download follows at most 5 redirects, must finish within 60 seconds, and may be at most 25 MB.
sections.heading: Only URLs, and which ones

sections.excerpt: For spreadsheets with many rows, combine the Excel parser with the sandbox tool: 1. Agent parses the Excel file to understand the structure 2. Agent writes a pandas script to process the full dataset 3. Sandbox executes the script and returns the results
sections.heading: Working with large spreadsheets

sections.excerpt: - .xlsx (Excel 2007+) — full support - .xls (Excel 97-2003) — not supported (convert to .xlsx first) - .csv — not supported (agents can read CSVs directly via vault or sandbox)

pages.description: One tool that answers \"what is the date\" and \"what date is next Friday\" — so an agent computes dates instead of guessing them.

sections.excerpt: Models are unreliable about the current date and worse at arithmetic on it. The time tool gives an agent a real answer.

One tool. It returns a 10-digit Unix timestamp for the current moment, or for a date described relative to it. Called with no arguments it answers "now". Add arguments to move from there. | Argument | Type | Does | |---|---|---| | timezone | string | IANA name — UTC, America/NewYork, Asia/Kolkata. Defaults to UTC | | days | number | Add N days | | weeks | number | Add N weeks | | months | number…
sections.heading: getdatetime [#gettime]

sections.excerpt: The order matters, and it is the part worth knowing: - weeks + weekday — the week offset is applied first, then the weekday is found in that week. is next week's Friday. - months + date — the month offset is applied first, then the day is taken from that month. is the 16th of next month. - month alone — goes to that month in the current year, or next year if it has already passed.

sections.excerpt: Agents do not always think to check the date. Tell them: This matters most for agents that write to calendars, file reports by date, or compute deadlines — the failure mode is silent, confidently wrong, and easy to miss in a run log.

pages.description: Govern what an agent may do with the tools it holds — by behaviour rather than by name, with a real gate instead of a sentence in a prompt.

sections.excerpt: Ticking a tool on an agent decides whether it has the tool. Tool policy decides what it may do with it. The two are different questions, and only having the first one caused real problems. runsqlquery is one door for SELECT and for DROP, so a name-based allowlist admits or refuses both together. The old workaround was to ask in the system prompt — "confirm with the user before any write query" —…

Tools declare what they do, and a policy speaks about those declarations. It has three rows, riskiest first: | On the screen | Category | Means | |---|---|---| | Tools that change data permanently | destructive | The tool declares that it modifies data in a way that cannot be undone | | Tools that reach outside this workspace | openworld | The tool declares that it talks to systems this workspace…

SynapseOrch treats it that way: - A third-party server saying "I am destructive" is believed. - A third-party server saying "I am safe" is not believed — a read-only claim is treated as undeclared. - SynapseOrch's own servers are declared in the repository and are believed either way.
